6 · Import a custom player

I successfully imported the custom player 3D model and rigged skeleton into the game engine pipeline. The mesh, textures, and animations mapped correctly without breaking the default bone hierarchy. I created a reusable asset import preset inside the engine. This automatically configures rigging settings, materials, and scale factors for any future custom characters added to the project. How do we optimize the texture resolution and polygon count of this custom player model to maintain a stable frame rate when multiple characters are on screen at once? I used Google Gemini to answer the question.

My interpretation

I implemented the core tracking mechanic for the bounty contracts, linking target NPCs to a dynamic UI board. I decided to use a vector-based distance check to update a compass indicator, showing the player the relative direction of their bounty target. The target spawning system accurately reads the contract data, instantiates the unique boss model at a designated waypoint, and triggers the "Wanted: Alive or Dead" UI prompt when the player enters the zone. What is the most efficient way to manage target pathfinding across large maps so they can actively flee or ambush the player without causing performance drops? I use Google Gemini to answer the question.

Engine, assets + technology

Engine: Unity. It’s free, lightweight, and has good beginner tutorials, so everyone can install it and start quickly. Language: Unity C#. It’s built into Godot and easy to read, so teammates can understand each other’s code. Packages/add-ons: Godot’s built-in 2D/3D tools (sprites, collision, UI nodes) so we don’t depend on extra downloads that might break. Assets: Free, license-friendly art and sound (for example from Kenney.nl or OpenGameArt), plus our own wanted-poster designs made in Canva or Figma. We chose free assets so we don’t have copyright problems. Who checks them: [Leah Aluni] checks that the engine and code run on every team member’s computer. [Nicolas Kuhnast] checks that every asset has a license that lets us use it. [George Arbache] tests the finished build after each change. Why we chose these: They’re free, beginner-friendly, and work well for a small team with limited time. Open question: Do we need any extra add-ons for saving scores, or is the built-in system enough? I used Claude to get the answer

Future reuse + credits

PlayerController script (our own code). Source: written by our team. Credit: none required, but we’ll keep our names in the code comments. GameManager and score system (our own code). Source: written by our team. Credit: none required. It can be reused for any game that tracks points or objectives. Bounty data structure (BountyTarget class). Source: our team. Credit: none required. We can swap in new characters, rewards, and difficulty levels for a new story. Free art and sound assets (for example from Kenney.nl or OpenGameArt). Source: the website and creator’s name, saved in a credits file. Credit: we’ll check each license, since some (CC0) need no credit and others (CC-BY) require us to name the creator. Our wanted-poster and menu designs (Canva or Figma). Source: our team. Credit: if we used Canva templates or stock elements, we’ll check Canva’s license terms before reusing them. I used Claude for my answer.

Huddle decisions + open questions

What the huddle board is: A shared space where our team writes down what we discussed, what we agreed on, and what we still need to figure out, so nobody has to rely on memory and everyone can see the same plan. Decisions we made: We will build the game in [Godot/Unity] using [GDScript/C#], because it’s free and beginner-friendly. We will keep the game small: at least 3 bounties, a score system, and a win or game over screen. We will use free, license-friendly assets and keep a credits file listing each source. Each person owns one part of the pipeline: [Name 1] inputs, [Name 2] building, [Name 3] design, [Name 4] testing. Disagreements: Some of us wanted more bounties and extra levels, while others wanted to finish a smaller game that works. We agreed to finish 3 bounties first and add more only if time is left. We discussed whether to draw our own art or use free assets. We chose free assets for the characters and made our own wanted posters. Questions that remain open: Do we need an extra add-on to save high scores, or is the built-in system enough? Who will double-check that every asset’s license allows us to reuse it? How many classmates can test the game before the deadline? I used Claude to get the answers
